nodes.title: Revisions
nodes.body:
1994 Jan 1. DMS|RGG; Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institution

note: There was no date on the original document so 1994 Jan 1 was assigned since most of the SLHs were prepared from 1994 thru 1997.

nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Common Name:  Summer flounder
Scientific Name:  Paralichthys dentatus

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum:  Chordata
	Class:  Osteichthyes
	Order:  Pleuronectiformes
	Family:  Bothidae

Other Common Names: Flounder, fluke, plaice

Other:	Reference for Scientific Name (Linnaeus 1766)
	Reference for Classification (Robins et al.1991)

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  Is a high quality food fish sought by both commercial and sport fishermen (Poole 1966; Smith 1973).  Abundance is greatest in the Mid-Atlantic Bight (MAB), between Cape Cod and Cape Hatteras, where this species supports one of the most important commercial and recreational fisheries (Mid -Atlantic Fishery Management Council 1988;  Rogers and Van Den Avyle 1983;  Malloy and Targett 1991). The commercial fishery is not substantial in the South Atlantic Bight (south of Cape Hatteras to Florida) (Rogers and Van Den Avyle 1983).

Recreational:  One of the most important  recreational fisheries (Smith 1973; Mid-Atlantic Fishery Management Council 1988;  Malloy and Targett 1991; Rogers and Van Den Avyle 1983).   Supports a minor fishery within the Indian River Lagoon during the winter months (RGG pers. obs).

Ecological Role:  The role of summer flounder in the ecosystem function and community dynamics has not been adequately addressed, but the adults are generally regarded as higher level carnivores and thus influence the relative abundance of a variety of prey species (Rogers and Van Den Avyle 1983).

Indicator:  Due to its role as a top predator summer flounder could reflect the presence of  heavy  metals and toxic compounds in the ecosystem.

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  The summer flounder is found in  estuarine and continental shelf waters along the Atlantic coast of the U.S. from Maine (possibly Canada) to Florida (Gutherz 1967; Gilmore 1977; Martin and Drewry 1978).  South western range limit to the northern Gulf of Mexico (Dery 1988).  Abundance is greatest in the Mid-Atlantic Bight (MAB), between Cape Cod and Cape Hatteras, where this species supports one of the most important commercial and recreational fisheries (Mid-Atlantic Fishery Management Council 1988) (Malloy and Targett 1991).

Within Study Area:    Found in the Indian River Lagoon system and near shore waters, and particularly abundant as adults during the fall and winter months (Anderson and Gehringer 1965; Powell et al. 1972; Gilmore 1977; RGG per obs.).

Movements and Migrations:  In the northern part of their range adults move offshore in the fall to spawn and overwinter. In the spring movement is toward shallower water and estuaries and remain in these areas until the fall migration (Smith 1973). Apparently there is a major movement of summer flounder from more northern locations during the fall and winter. This southerly movement is accompanied by a major increase in Indian River Lagoon populations which are caught in the local recreational fishery (RGG per. obs.).

nodes.title: Life Mode
nodes.body: Benthic predator found in estuarine and near shore continental shelf waters.

nodes.title: BENTHIC HABITAT
nodes.body:
Habitat Type:   In the northern portion of their range adults are found during the winter in offshore waters to 100 fathoms, but generally 29 fathoms or less (Gutherz 1967).  Found during  the summer in estuaries and coastal waters over sand, mud, hard bottoms, seagrass and near pilings (Martin and Drewry 1978).   In North Carolina the post larvae settle during the winter in tidal flats in sandy bottom areas, in the spring the young move into the high salinity salt marsh habitats (Burke et al 1991).  Young summer flounder prefer mixed or sandy substrates with a high preference for  sandy substrates (Powell and Schwartz 1977;  Burke et al. 1991).  Juveniles are rare in the Indian River Lagoon (Gilmore 1988).  While adults are principally taken within the estuary during the fall and winter (RGG pers. obs.).

Substrate: sand, mud, hard bottoms, seagrass, salt marshes and near pilings (Powell and Schwartz 1977; Martin and Drewry 1978;  Burke et al. 1991; Szedlmayer et al. 1992).

nodes.title: Physical/Chemical
nodes.body:
Salinity: Summer flounder prefer the high salinity areas (Deubler and White 1962; Powell and Schwartz 1977;  Burke et al. 1991).  Salinity is a controlling factor in the growth of the summer flounder (Deubler and White 1962).
Temperature: Spawning occurs in water temperatures between 12 and 19 C (Smith 1973).  Settling larvae have been recorded at 2 C (Szedlmayer et al. 1992) and a 100% survival rate at 3  C  for juveniles (Malloy and Target 1991).  Summer flounder grow best at high salinity and moderate temperature (Peters 1971).

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Reproductive Mode:  Gonochoristic, serial spawners, oviparous, iteroparous (Morse 1981).

Mating/Spawning:: Spawning begins after the fall migration to deeper waters (Smith 1973). Spawning occurs in water temperatures between 12 and 19 C (Smith 1973). Spawning begins north of Chesapeake Bay  as early as September and continues through November.  From Chesapeake Bay south to North Carolina spawning starts in November and continues through February (Smith 1973).  In the South Atlantic Bight spawning starts in late November and continues through early spring (Morse 1981; Rogers and Van Den Avyle 1983;  Able et al. 1990).  High egg production is maintained by shedding batches of eggs rather than shedding eggs all at once, with eggs making up 40-50% of the  spawning female biomass (Morse 1991).

Spawning Strategy:  is a combination of extended spawning season with variable duration, early maturation (age two or three), high fecundity, serial spawning and extensive migrations across the continental shelf during spawning" (Morse 1981). The reproductive strategy of summer flounder tends to maximize reproductive potential and avoid catastrophe.

Fecundity: Morse (1981) estimates fecundity for fish between 366 and 680 mm TL to range from 463,000 to 4,188,00 ova.

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Egg:  The eggs of the summer flounder are found in the near surface waters and range in diameter from 0.90 to 1.13 mm with a mean of 1.02 mm.  The yolk is translucent amber in reflected light and opaque white in transmitted light.  The egg has one oil droplet of 0.18 to 0.31 mm in diameter (Martin and Drewry 1978; Smith and Fahay 1970).

Larvae:  Hatching of larval flounder occurs at 2.41-2.82 mm notochord length.  Yolk is absorbed by 3.16 mm SL; eye migration begins as early as 9.5 mm; and metamorphosis is complete by approximately 15 mm SL (Smith and Fahay 1979; Martin and Drewry 1978).

Juvenile:  The Juveniles remain in the shallow estuaries for the first 18-20 months in the tidal flats (Powell and Schwartz 1977) and in marshes and creeks (Szedlmayer et al. 1992).  After 18-20 months, the yearlings move out to the shelf waters in the fall (Powell and Schwartz 1977).  The young of the year 160-320 mm move out with the adults in the fall to shelf waters (Able et al. 1990).  In the first year,  juveniles can grow at a rate from 1.9 to 2.0 mm/day or reach a size of 200-326 mm (Able et al. 1990; Malloy and Targett 1991;  Szedlmayer et al. 1992).

Adult:  The adults exhibit sexual dimorphism  with the females maturing at a larger size than the males.  The minimum length for maturity, 24-27 cm TL for males and 30-33 cm TL for females (Morse 1981).  Maximum size for males reported 55-65 cm and 80 cm for females (Poole 1966).  Summer flounder may live to ten years, all specimens over seven years were female  (Roger and Van Den Avyle 1983).

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body: Summer flounder are sight feeders and can equally capture prey in the water column or on the bottom (Olla et al. 1972).  The young summer flounder 100-200 mm TL feeds on mysid shrimp and fish with mysids in greater abundance, while as size increases decapod crustaceans and fish are consumed in similar quantities (Powell and Schwartz 1979).  Smith and Daiber (1977) found that specimens under 45 cm fed mostly on invertebrates while, larger specimens consumed more fish.

nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body:
Predation:  The role of summer flounder in the ecosystem function and community dynamics has not been adequately addressed, but the adults are generally regarded as higher level carnivores and thus influence the relative abundance of a variety of prey species (Rogers and Van Den Avyle 1983).

Factors influencing populations:  Fishery pressures, habitat loss and water temperatures.

sections.heading: HEADER
sections.content:
Title:  Summer flounder (Paralichthys dentatus)

FLELMR Code:  2991

sections.heading: Revisions
sections.content:
1994 Jan 1. DMS|RGG; Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institution

note: There was no date on the original document so 1994 Jan 1 was assigned since most of the SLHs were prepared from 1994 thru 1997.

sections.heading: TAXONOMY
sections.content:
Common Name:  Summer flounder
Scientific Name:  Paralichthys dentatus

sections.heading: Classification
sections.content:
Phylum:  Chordata
	Class:  Osteichthyes
	Order:  Pleuronectiformes
	Family:  Bothidae

Other Common Names: Flounder, fluke, plaice

Other:	Reference for Scientific Name (Linnaeus 1766)
	Reference for Classification (Robins et al.1991)

sections.heading: VALUE & STATUS
sections.content:
Commercial:  Is a high quality food fish sought by both commercial and sport fishermen (Poole 1966; Smith 1973).  Abundance is greatest in the Mid-Atlantic Bight (MAB), between Cape Cod and Cape Hatteras, where this species supports one of the most important commercial and recreational fisheries (Mid -Atlantic Fishery Management Council 1988;  Rogers and Van Den Avyle 1983;  Malloy and Targett 1991). The commercial fishery is not substantial in the South Atlantic Bight (south of Cape Hatteras to Florida) (Rogers and Van Den Avyle 1983).

Recreational:  One of the most important  recreational fisheries (Smith 1973; Mid-Atlantic Fishery Management Council 1988;  Malloy and Targett 1991; Rogers and Van Den Avyle 1983).   Supports a minor fishery within the Indian River Lagoon during the winter months (RGG pers. obs).

Ecological Role:  The role of summer flounder in the ecosystem function and community dynamics has not been adequately addressed, but the adults are generally regarded as higher level carnivores and thus influence the relative abundance of a variety of prey species (Rogers and Van Den Avyle 1983).

Indicator:  Due to its role as a top predator summer flounder could reflect the presence of  heavy  metals and toxic compounds in the ecosystem.

sections.heading: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
sections.content:
Overall:  The summer flounder is found in  estuarine and continental shelf waters along the Atlantic coast of the U.S. from Maine (possibly Canada) to Florida (Gutherz 1967; Gilmore 1977; Martin and Drewry 1978).  South western range limit to the northern Gulf of Mexico (Dery 1988).  Abundance is greatest in the Mid-Atlantic Bight (MAB), between Cape Cod and Cape Hatteras, where this species supports one of the most important commercial and recreational fisheries (Mid-Atlantic Fishery Management Council 1988) (Malloy and Targett 1991).

Within Study Area:    Found in the Indian River Lagoon system and near shore waters, and particularly abundant as adults during the fall and winter months (Anderson and Gehringer 1965; Powell et al. 1972; Gilmore 1977; RGG per obs.).

Movements and Migrations:  In the northern part of their range adults move offshore in the fall to spawn and overwinter. In the spring movement is toward shallower water and estuaries and remain in these areas until the fall migration (Smith 1973). Apparently there is a major movement of summer flounder from more northern locations during the fall and winter. This southerly movement is accompanied by a major increase in Indian River Lagoon populations which are caught in the local recreational fishery (RGG per. obs.).

sections.heading: Life Mode
sections.content: Benthic predator found in estuarine and near shore continental shelf waters.

sections.heading: BENTHIC HABITAT
sections.content:
Habitat Type:   In the northern portion of their range adults are found during the winter in offshore waters to 100 fathoms, but generally 29 fathoms or less (Gutherz 1967).  Found during  the summer in estuaries and coastal waters over sand, mud, hard bottoms, seagrass and near pilings (Martin and Drewry 1978).   In North Carolina the post larvae settle during the winter in tidal flats in sandy bottom areas, in the spring the young move into the high salinity salt marsh habitats (Burke et al 1991).  Young summer flounder prefer mixed or sandy substrates with a high preference for  sandy substrates (Powell and Schwartz 1977;  Burke et al. 1991).  Juveniles are rare in the Indian River Lagoon (Gilmore 1988).  While adults are principally taken within the estuary during the fall and winter (RGG pers. obs.).

Substrate: sand, mud, hard bottoms, seagrass, salt marshes and near pilings (Powell and Schwartz 1977; Martin and Drewry 1978;  Burke et al. 1991; Szedlmayer et al. 1992).

sections.heading: Physical/Chemical
sections.content:
Salinity: Summer flounder prefer the high salinity areas (Deubler and White 1962; Powell and Schwartz 1977;  Burke et al. 1991).  Salinity is a controlling factor in the growth of the summer flounder (Deubler and White 1962).
Temperature: Spawning occurs in water temperatures between 12 and 19 C (Smith 1973).  Settling larvae have been recorded at 2 C (Szedlmayer et al. 1992) and a 100% survival rate at 3  C  for juveniles (Malloy and Target 1991).  Summer flounder grow best at high salinity and moderate temperature (Peters 1971).

sections.heading: REPRODUCTION
sections.content:
Reproductive Mode:  Gonochoristic, serial spawners, oviparous, iteroparous (Morse 1981).

Mating/Spawning:: Spawning begins after the fall migration to deeper waters (Smith 1973). Spawning occurs in water temperatures between 12 and 19 C (Smith 1973). Spawning begins north of Chesapeake Bay  as early as September and continues through November.  From Chesapeake Bay south to North Carolina spawning starts in November and continues through February (Smith 1973).  In the South Atlantic Bight spawning starts in late November and continues through early spring (Morse 1981; Rogers and Van Den Avyle 1983;  Able et al. 1990).  High egg production is maintained by shedding batches of eggs rather than shedding eggs all at once, with eggs making up 40-50% of the  spawning female biomass (Morse 1991).

Spawning Strategy:  is a combination of extended spawning season with variable duration, early maturation (age two or three), high fecundity, serial spawning and extensive migrations across the continental shelf during spawning" (Morse 1981). The reproductive strategy of summer flounder tends to maximize reproductive potential and avoid catastrophe.

Fecundity: Morse (1981) estimates fecundity for fish between 366 and 680 mm TL to range from 463,000 to 4,188,00 ova.

sections.heading: Length Range
sections.content:
Egg:  The eggs of the summer flounder are found in the near surface waters and range in diameter from 0.90 to 1.13 mm with a mean of 1.02 mm.  The yolk is translucent amber in reflected light and opaque white in transmitted light.  The egg has one oil droplet of 0.18 to 0.31 mm in diameter (Martin and Drewry 1978; Smith and Fahay 1970).

Larvae:  Hatching of larval flounder occurs at 2.41-2.82 mm notochord length.  Yolk is absorbed by 3.16 mm SL; eye migration begins as early as 9.5 mm; and metamorphosis is complete by approximately 15 mm SL (Smith and Fahay 1979; Martin and Drewry 1978).

Juvenile:  The Juveniles remain in the shallow estuaries for the first 18-20 months in the tidal flats (Powell and Schwartz 1977) and in marshes and creeks (Szedlmayer et al. 1992).  After 18-20 months, the yearlings move out to the shelf waters in the fall (Powell and Schwartz 1977).  The young of the year 160-320 mm move out with the adults in the fall to shelf waters (Able et al. 1990).  In the first year,  juveniles can grow at a rate from 1.9 to 2.0 mm/day or reach a size of 200-326 mm (Able et al. 1990; Malloy and Targett 1991;  Szedlmayer et al. 1992).

Adult:  The adults exhibit sexual dimorphism  with the females maturing at a larger size than the males.  The minimum length for maturity, 24-27 cm TL for males and 30-33 cm TL for females (Morse 1981).  Maximum size for males reported 55-65 cm and 80 cm for females (Poole 1966).  Summer flounder may live to ten years, all specimens over seven years were female  (Roger and Van Den Avyle 1983).

sections.heading: FOOD HABITS
sections.content: Summer flounder are sight feeders and can equally capture prey in the water column or on the bottom (Olla et al. 1972).  The young summer flounder 100-200 mm TL feeds on mysid shrimp and fish with mysids in greater abundance, while as size increases decapod crustaceans and fish are consumed in similar quantities (Powell and Schwartz 1979).  Smith and Daiber (1977) found that specimens under 45 cm fed mostly on invertebrates while, larger specimens consumed more fish.

sections.heading: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
sections.content:
Predation:  The role of summer flounder in the ecosystem function and community dynamics has not been adequately addressed, but the adults are generally regarded as higher level carnivores and thus influence the relative abundance of a variety of prey species (Rogers and Van Den Avyle 1983).

Factors influencing populations:  Fishery pressures, habitat loss and water temperatures.
